item.description:
time is a POSIX utility for timing commands. Most shells build it in, and Zsh’s version has a lot more to offer than the one in Bash.

Put time before a command to time it. For example, to time a Python script:

$ time python example.py
python example.py …

item.title: [andros.dev] I got banned from Lobsters for writing like an LLM
item.description:
I've been banned from Lobsters. If you're bored, you can read about my experience.

If you don't know it, Lobsters is a news aggregator focused on technology and computing, although other topics of general interest also come up. The most interesting part is the comments on each thread or link, where the topics are discussed. As alternatives, there are Hacker News, Lemmy and, to some extent, Reddit.

To give you some background, I've been a Lobsters user for a few years. I've contributed comments and links, and I'm also the author of the Emacs client. On top of that, the IRC channel I hang out in the most is #lobsters on Libera.Chat.

Chapter 1: Your domain has been blocked

A year ago, around Christmas 2025, I tried to share an article on Lobsters. My usual style, educational but fun. When I did, I ran into a warning telling me that my website's domain was blocked for self-promotion. My domain?

This surprised me, since I hadn't shared content from my website on Lobsters before, and I had read the odd unhappy comment. But blocking the whole domain seemed a bit much.

I didn't make a big deal of it! I sent an email to the moderators explaining the situation.

I got no reply.

Chapter 2: Contributing again

Almost a year later, with a few articles on the Hacker News front page, I thought about Lobsters again.

I decided to contribute again with a simple post: my experience building a modern BBS. Improvements over older systems like BBJ, and an explanation of some design decisions.

It ended with an invitation to try it, and I shared it with the show tag. Nothing more.

Same result: domain blocked for self-promotion. They hadn't lifted the block after a year, and they never answered my message.

I didn't make a big deal of it.

By chance, I found a way to post a blocked domain. It looked like a small bug.

I was posting again after a year in exile.

Chapter 3: The rise

Little by little, the points went up and the comments came in, nothing out of the ordinary. At 8 points I could see it on the front page.

I took my time to reply; the conversation was constructive. One user even found a design flaw. Fantastic! But... the joy didn't last long.

Soon after, the trouble started.

Chapter 4: Down the well

Several users accused me of using AI, not in my code but in my replies to the comments. One of them even included a link where an external service claimed that one of my replies was 100% AI-generated.

The evidence was irrefutable.

According to the tool, there wasn't the slightest doubt. I started to doubt my own self-awareness. What if I was an LLM and didn't know it?

Obviously I replied that it wasn't true (probably not). But the damage was done. Other users joined in with similar accusations, and the snowball kept rolling and getting bigger and bigger. They even called me a self-promotion bot! My existence had less and less dignity.

When I asked why they thought I was an LLM, I got a detailed explanation.

The number of users flagging the thread as spam kept growing. The situation became unsustainable.

The greyed-out, faded color means the thread has been hidden by many users.

If you try to open the thread now, you won't be able to unless you have an account. So how do I have screenshots? Well, that's a topic for another article.

I sent an urgent message to a moderator with the subject "Help!", along with a short explanation.

Again, I got no reply.

Some time later, with all hope lost, I saw a notification in the Lobsters menu. I had a new message, this time from a moderator.

Your story has been removed for breaking the community rules. Self-promotional content is not allowed.

My face was a picture when I read it.

It came with a link to the community rules, specifically this section:

Self-promotion: It's great to have authors participate in the community, but not to exploit it as a write-only tool for product announcements or driving traffic to their work. As a rule of thumb, self-promo should be less than a quarter of one's stories and comments in the last year. New users (first 70 days) are not allowed to submit self-promo.

Now I made a big deal of it!

I replied, asking where the fine line was between sharing knowledge and self-promotion, and whether there was any way to appeal the decision. The answer was that I had to improve my ratio of what they considered self-promotion.

Okay, I committed to it. I would write more comments and fewer links. It could be a discussion forum for me.

But the hardest blow was yet to come.

Chapter 5: Your account has been banned

Two hours later, I got the following message in my personal email:

Subject: [Lobsters] account X banned

You have been banned from Lobsters by ** ** ** For:

Only self-promo, slop.

You are no longer allowed to login to the site. If you wish, you can discuss this ban with the moderator by replying to this e-mail.

What happened? I thought the matter had been cleared up and settled.

I replied. I wasn't going to miss the chance to appeal the decision:

Hi *******,

I think there has been a misunderstanding.

[Here was an explanation of what happened]

[Here were my interactions with the moderators]

It has been an unfortunate situation, and I felt completely helpless.

At this point, could my account be reactivated? I don't think I'll find the courage to share more content after what happened, but I'd still like to contribute in the comments. I'm an active user on IRC. Also, I'd rather not live with the cognitive dissonance of maintaining an Emacs client for an aggregator/community I've been banned from.

Best regards

And the answer? The usual: silence, and nothing more.

Epilogue

Some questions are still on my mind. Will they be able to read me? If my domain is blocked, a regular user won't be able to submit this article, let alone comment on it (unless they use the same trick). Will they ever answer my messages? What would happen if I ran their own comments through the same AI detector?

On the other hand, it seems that writing long, detailed replies has become dangerous. Not long ago, when you took the time to write a careful text, with references or quotes, it was received with respect and admiration. Although you ran the risk of coming across as pretentious and pedantic. Today, however, the trend is short replies, without punctuation or embellishments. If you want to prove you're human, you have to write like a teenager chatting with their friends.

As for the moderation, I'm nobody to judge anyone. Who do you favor when there are problems? Individual users, or the group that contributes content and keeps the site alive? Maybe we would have done the same in their place, or maybe we would have tried to mediate. Who knows! There are also many variables we don't know. Still, silence is not pleasant.

If they lifted the ban, would I come back? Yes, but only to comment. My content fits better elsewhere, and that's fine. Every community has its own rules.

And for everything else... Hacker News, Reddit and other forums.

Help me keep writing Every coffee gives me a push toward the next article. Sure, it's on me!

Send an email to comment+article-94a77341@andros.dev to leave a comment. The subject will be ignored.

item.title: [www.eferro.net] Building got cheap. Complexity didn't
item.description:
If you've read me before, you know where I stand: most of our job is learning how things work while we keep complexity under control. This post is a concrete example of how I've been designing and building things lately, trying to keep complexity as low as I can and the cost of each solution small. The idea is simple. Every decision that can be postponed gets postponed, until the moment we actually need to build it.

In Turning up the dial I described the workspace where I do this kind of work, and promised to take it apart piece by piece. Consider this the first piece. Everything in this post happened in there, from the skills I used to the task file where the postponed decisions still live. That post was about the system. This one follows a single feature through it, from the first question to the first real users.

The interesting part isn't the idea. It's the flow, the tools, and the list of decisions we didn't take.

Why this matters more now

AI has removed a lot of friction from building. It also helps a bit with understanding code and systems we don't know; I can get a decent map of an unfamiliar repo in a few minutes. But the amount of complexity a team can hold in its head, operate, debug at three in the morning and change without fear is about the same as it was. Maybe a little more with better tools. Not much more.

We are still the bottleneck. Every streaming connection, every subscription model, every cache adds to the basal cost of a system, the part you keep paying whether anyone uses the feature or not. When writing code was slow, that cost hid behind the effort. Now the code appears quickly, and the complexity stays with us.

So the useful question has changed. It's no longer "can we build it?". It's "what's the least we can build to find out if it deserves more?".

The case

We're removing Slack as the place where our platform talks to people. Alarms, the progress of long operations (creating an application, for example) and personal notices go through a small notification service that, until now, delivered everything to Slack. Some colleagues, who joined from another company, don't use Slack at all. When they create an application from our CLI they get "submitted"... and then nothing.

The feature: let people read their notifications from the CLI.

One more piece of context, because it changes how you should read every number below. I don't code full time. Between meetings, people and everything else, development gets maybe 10–15% of my focus on a good day. So when I say something took a day and a half, that's calendar time at my pace, in the gaps. Someone working on this with full focus would have needed a fraction of that.

This is what the whole thing looked like, from the first question to feedback from real users:

Step 1. Diverge, on purpose

I started a Claude Code session with the grilling skill (from Matt Pocock's skills, I keep a copy in my skill-factory repo). It interviews you about a plan, one question at a time, each with options and a recommendation, until nothing important is left implicit. I asked for exactly that format: one question, a few options, I pick or I write my own answer.

25 questions in 21 minutes.

And here's the part I'm not proud of. Claude's first recommendations were the narrow ones: store only operation feedback, address only people. I was the one who widened the scope. "Everything". "Person, team or topic". Then I threw in an analogy ("how does kubectl do it for events?") and the design grew a server-side stream. Twenty minutes later I had a beautiful system on the table: streaming like kubectl get -w, topics people could subscribe to, read state per message plus a watermark, alarm grouping, an unread counter cached in the background, a neutral message format with a new Slack renderer on top.

None of it was unreasonable. With an agent writing most of the code, I could probably have built all of it in a couple of weeks. That's exactly the problem.

I don't think the divergence was a mistake, though. You need to see the whole problem before you can decide what to leave out. The mistake would have been to stop there.

Step 2. Converge, also on purpose

So I switched tools. I asked for two skills together: complexity-review and hamburger-method. My prompt was, more or less, "find which points add a lot of complexity at the start, how we could solve them, and a much simpler approach".

complexity-review is a skill I wrote that checks a design against 30 dimensions of complexity (state, consistency, latency, dependencies, security, lifespan...) and pushes for the simplest option that works. It found eight drivers in my design. What made it useful wasn't the list. It was the shape of each row: the complex thing, a simpler option, and when to add it.

Streaming became polling every three seconds, "until polling load or latency is a measured problem". Grouping got postponed with a number next to it: around 1,300 alerts in four months is about 11 a day, so "add it when one recipient gets more than ~50 a day". Topics would wait "until a real group needs a channel that is not a team". It also gave a rough guess of the ongoing cost: 15–20% of the team's capacity for my design, 3–5% for the simple one. Those are Claude's estimates, not measurements. I didn't need them to be precise. The order of magnitude was enough.

The hamburger method is Gojko Adzic's technique for slicing a feature vertically; my skill is just a way to apply it systematically. You split the feature into the steps it goes through (the layers of the burger), list several options for each layer from "almost nothing" to "the full thing", and then pick one option per layer so that every slice works end to end. Here it was five layers with five options each:



Slice 1 is the green path. Store every message the service already receives in one Postgres table. Show people their own messages and their teams'. Reuse the existing API key plus an identity token. A plain list command in the CLI. No read state at all; if you want recent stuff, use --since. Estimated at 2–3 days.

Claude proposed slice 1 plus three more cards for the next slices. I went further: one card, slice 1 only, "and write down under what conditions we'd fill in each of the initial decisions, if that time ever comes".

That sentence is the heart of this post.

Step 3. Write down the triggers

The ideas from the divergent phase didn't go to the bin. They went to a table in the task: the postponed decision, the design we had already agreed on in case we build it, and the trigger that tells us it's time. By the end of the work the table had sixteen rows. Here are some of them, with what happened next:

Postponed Slice 1 does instead Trigger to build it What happened
Server streaming List only Polling load or latency is a measured problem Waiting
Live follow by polling List only Someone needs to watch messages live Fired on day 2
Identity-only route API key + identity token The shared key must stop reaching clients Fired on day 3
Read state (one watermark per person) None, filter with --since Daily use makes "what's new" hard to see Waiting
Alarm grouping One row per delivery One recipient gets > ~50 a day (measured then: ~11) Waiting
Topics Unrouted messages go to the owning team A group needs a channel that isn't a team Waiting
Map GitLab users to directory ids Store the id as it comes, log a warning The warnings show a real gap Gap measured: 107 of 138 GitLab messages go to a bot
Retention (90 days) Keep everything ~1M rows, or before general availability Waiting

Writing this table changed how converging felt. Cutting scope usually feels like losing something. Here nothing was lost: the design was there, agreed and written down, waiting for a reason. It also makes the conversation with yourself (or with your team) much shorter the day someone says "we should add topics". Fine. Has the trigger happened?

Step 4. Make the change easy

Before building the slice, I asked Claude to look at the current architecture of the service and prepare it for the feature, using two more skills: thin-wrappers (wrap each piece of infrastructure behind a small interface in the language of the domain) and hexagonal-architecture. It found five problems. The most telling one: the ports were shaped like Slack. Routing only knew Slack targets. If I had added the inbox on top of that, the inbox would have inherited Slack's concepts forever.

That turned into six preparation steps with no new behaviour: domain ports, the GitLab webhook going through the same path as every other message, a shared Postgres base, migrations. About a day of work.

It's the old Kent Beck line: "for each desired change, make the change easy (warning: this may be hard), then make the easy change". I'll be honest, this is also where the method gets a bit uncomfortable. That day was design work done before the slice existed, which is precisely what the rest of this post tells you to avoid. My take is that it's a different kind of design: it doesn't add capabilities, it removes friction from the next change. But I can see someone arguing the other way.

Step 5. Make the easy change

Then the slice itself, in small safe steps (yes, there's a skill for that too). 35 commits in the service and 7 in the CLI between the 19th and the 21st, every push going through the pipeline to production. The database code went to production inert first, with nothing calling it; then the database declaration; then the wiring; then the recording, live on the morning of the 20th. With mutation testing on the pieces that mattered: 46 mutants on the component that records messages, all killed, and two of them found real gaps before production did.

Slice 1 was storing real messages about 38 hours after the design session, and readable from the CLI that same evening. Inside the 2–3 day estimate, and that's with a small slice of my day. With full focus it would have been hours, not days. I think that's the part that surprised me most: the thin slice is so small that even part-time it reaches production before the week is over.

Step 6. Let production decide what's next

Two triggers fired in the first 72 hours.

The first was live follow. I wanted to watch my notifications while an operation ran, so polling moved from the table into the same task as a second slice. The trigger wasn't a metric; it was a user asking. That user was me. I'm fine with that, but it's worth saying.

The second one was more interesting. For the colleagues without Slack, the CLI couldn't depend on a shared API key they'd never have. That was exactly the trigger we had written: "the shared key must stop reaching clients". Before opening the new route we measured what it would cost to abuse it (every forged token meant one request to the identity provider: 50 fake tokens, 50 requests) and added a limit. The design was already in the table. Building it took a morning, a part-time one.

Then came real users. Seven engineers without Slack created test applications with the CLI open in another terminal, following their notifications. One wrote "all good, it took around 30s for the first message to appear". Another: "within a few seconds". Each run produced about eight messages, addressed to the right person.

And real use found things no design session would have found. With no Slack account, the service fell back to a shared Slack channel, so about 37 of their messages also landed in a place nobody expected. One path stored messages for a username that wasn't a person in our directory, so nobody could ever read them. And 107 of 138 GitLab messages were addressed to a bot. That last one was already a row in the table. Now it has a number.

What I'm less sure about

The feedback came from a guided beta that lasted a couple of days, not from people using this every morning. A week later I have no data showing daily use. The check "you see your messages and nobody else sees them" is proven by the data, not by a second person actually trying. And none of the other triggers have fired. Maybe the slice is enough. Maybe nobody uses it enough to need more. I don't know yet, and I'd rather say it.

I'm also aware that the design ended up simple because I asked for it to be simple, after letting it grow. The skills didn't decide anything. They made it cheap to open the space and then cheap to close it again. The table made closing it feel less like losing.

So

Diverge to see the whole problem. Converge to the thinnest slice that works end to end. Don't throw away what you saw: write each postponed decision next to the trigger that brings it back, with a number measured today if you can. Make the change easy, then make it. And let production tell you which row comes next.

None of this is new. Vertical slicing and the last responsible moment are old ideas. What's new is the pressure. When an agent can turn the whole divergent design into working code by Friday, the discipline to converge is about the only thing between us and a system bigger than we can understand.

Which leaves me with a question: now that building the full version costs almost nothing, how many of the features we ship will be just a divergent phase that nobody bothered to converge?

Related reading

  • Turning up the dial: seeing the forest while working on any tree, the workspace and way of working this flow lives in
  • Encoding Experience into AI Skills
  • Gojko Adzic, Splitting user stories: the hamburger method
  • My skills: eferro/skill-factory (complexity-review, hamburger-method, small-safe-steps, thin-wrappers, hexagonal-architecture, mutation-testing)
  • Matt Pocock's skills, where grilling comes from
  • Kent Beck, "make the change easy, then make the easy change"
  • The Art of Small Steps in Software Development: A Lean Vision

item.title: [www.eferro.net] Turning up the dial: seeing the forest while working on any tree
item.description:
First post in a series about how I work at Clarity AI with an AI-native workspace. This one covers the experiment and the way of working; the next ones go deeper into specific pieces.

The forest problem

In April I decided to try to see the whole forest and still work on any tree, in any repo, owned by any team, without giving up on quality or on small, safe, sustainable steps. This post is how that went.

As Head of Engineering and Data Platform at Clarity AI, I have to look at the whole system all the time: dozens of repositories, many teams, data pipelines that depend on other data pipelines. If I only look at one repo, I miss what matters. If I only look at the whole, I lose contact with the code, and with it the ability to judge whether what we’re doing makes sense. The usual way out is a trade-off: you see the forest (meetings, documents, dashboards) and stop touching the trees, or you get into one tree and only hear about the rest secondhand. For years I lived somewhere in between, never comfortably.



The experiment: turning up the dial

Kent Beck described Extreme Programming as taking the practices that already work and turning the dial all the way up. If code reviews are good, review all the time. If testing is good, test all the time.

My experiment has two dials that move together. One is the practices I’ve trusted for years: small safe steps, TDD, trunk-based development, everything versioned, checking changes in the running system instead of stopping at the merge. The other is how much work I delegate to AI agents. What I’ve seen so far is that the second dial can only go as high as the first: delegating more without stronger practices just means breaking things faster. That’s an observation from one person over nearly six months, not something I’ve measured, and the rest of the post is the evidence I have for it, including where it falls short.



It started on 16 April 2026 as a git repository just for me, which I called platform-office, with a first commit called “bootstrap platform-office AI-native workspace”. The idea was modest: a place where an agent could find everything it needed, so I could stop re-explaining context in every session. The agents are Claude Code sessions, and the co-author trailers in the commits record which model made each change, and it changed over those months.

The mantra: everything is in the repo

One rule shaped everything else: if it’s not in the repo, it doesn’t exist.

That covers code, tasks, decisions, knowledge, communications with other teams, incidents, recaps, the skills the agents use, the tools those skills call, and even the engineering practices, packaged as skills. The company’s code repositories are not inside; they’re cloned when a task needs them. What I ended up with is a single repository for all the context around the code.

The first commit already had tasks/, decisions/, knowledge/ and five skills to manage them. Today it holds hundreds of tasks, decision records and knowledge documents, plus tracked communications, incidents and 45 skills, all plain Markdown with YAML front matter, readable by a person and parseable by an agent.


Writing all of that down is what lets an agent pick up any thread from a five-word prompt, and a colleague pick it up without asking me.

Keeping it that way meant going against the defaults. Agent harnesses like Claude Code (the program that runs the agent and enforces its permissions and hooks) save what the agent learns as personal memory, one user at a time. I wanted that knowledge to belong to the team and to anyone using the repo, so I had to be explicit: in August the agents were told to write what they learn into files in the repo, and a check blocks the commit if an instruction file points to private memory. On 10 September I moved the last personal memories worth keeping into the repo. A week later a colleague committed a piece of knowledge with the message “out of one laptop’s memory”.



How the work gets done: the skill families

A skill, as I use it here, is a flow with phases and gates (points where it stops and waits for a human decision), backed by deterministic tools in the same repo. There are 45, and they cluster into a few families: orienting the agent in the current state of the work, driving a task from capture to close, operations and incidents, the data platform, knowledge and decisions, cross-team communications, code quality, and setup and housekeeping. Several come from the practice skills I wrote about in Encoding Experience into AI Skills.

In practice, a session starts with a short sentence. Some kick off a flow: “run task X”, “look at this alert”, “let’s do a recap of what happened this week”. Others are open questions: “explain how system X works”, “let’s look at how we could improve the architecture of Y”. Either way, the agent loads the context it needs from the repo. It also looks up our organization inventory (more on it below) to find the code repositories related to the request, and clones them when it needs to read the code to give a better answer. Then it keeps working until it needs a decision from me.

Three of them are worth describing in more detail.

The task skill, po-do-task, runs a task through 14 phases and stops for a human decision only where it matters: before implementing, committing, pushing or talking to another team. The phases are: identify, take ownership, clarify, propose alternatives, implement with TDD, mutation testing, test desiderata, report, commit, push, watch CI, validate in the running system, close, and a mandatory postmortem, where the agent reviews what went wrong in the run and proposes changes to the skill itself. Those changes go back into the skill, which several people have rewritten many times.

The incident skill takes a single trigger (a Slack link, a failing pipeline, a pasted alert) through hypotheses and validation, works back from the immediate cause to the systemic one, and ends with follow-up tasks and a postmortem.

The summary skills look at a window of time instead of a single alarm. A census of the Kubernetes event stream complements alerting: it looks for steady signals that never cross a threshold, and proposes which ones deserve a closer look. A weekly health check runs five sources in parallel and crosses them. The manual sweep behind it found its best signal in that crossing: Airflow DAG issues clustering in the same afternoon window as memory pressure in a heavy batch process, which neither source showed on its own.

The principles, in practice

Looking back, the principles I wanted to follow show up in the commits.

See the forest

One repo holds the context of the whole platform, and the code repos a task needs are a command away. It didn’t start that way: I began with git submodules, and by late June there were dozens of them, copied again into every worktree, and the repo had become slow and heavy. On 12 July a decision record replaced them with plain clones on demand.

One code repository is the exception: our organization inventory, present in every session. It’s where Clarity keeps its governance data: dozens of teams and the repositories, Airflow DAGs, container images, Kubernetes deployments, S3 buckets, runtime applications and models each one owns, kept up to date automatically. The workspace reads it instead of copying it. So the first questions of any investigation are cheap: which repositories, applications and data pipelines relate to this topic, and which teams work on it. Even the catalogue of repos and the list of people who can own a task come from there.

Work on any tree

A task registered here is ours to finish, even when the fix lives in another team’s repository. The default is to diagnose the root cause, make the change and coordinate with the owners, with a tracked communication so they’re never surprised, rather than to open a ticket for them. The workspace brings the context; each repository keeps its own rules. A change in someone else’s repo follows that repo’s conventions, CI, review process and owners, in the same small steps as everything else.

Small, safe, sustainable steps

Two weeks in, the pre-commit hook was already running the whole test suite, and the workspace’s own tooling was being hardened with mutation testing. Everything goes trunk-based. Some things stay deliberately slow: any destructive change to live infrastructure is run by a person, one command at a time. The agent writes the exact command; a human runs it and reads the output.

Agents have no access of their own. They work with the access of whoever starts the session, and the rules every session loads keep the important steps in human hands: nothing is pushed, or sent to Slack or to another team, without an explicit go, and when someone approves a specific command, that exact command is what runs.

Experimentation and impact

From the first commit, every task declares its why and can be framed as a hypothesis. In May a validating state appeared: a merged change stays open until it’s checked in the running system. In August came discarded, because a well-argued “we’re not doing this” is also a result; 128 tasks have been discarded on purpose so far.

Learning

Corrections become rules or tools, and sometimes the right call is neither. In July I swept the agent sessions for repeated frictions and the conclusion was clear: rules that live only in documentation get violated; rules enforced by the harness, through hooks and checks, get followed. So corrections keep moving from text into checks, as the next section shows.

When the system got it wrong

Few of the failures I found were an agent doing something silly. Most were the system breaking in ways I hadn’t designed for, and more often than not it was the agent itself, in the mandatory postmortem, who noticed. Three patterns keep coming back.

Rules written as text get ignored; rules turned into tools get followed. A rule that said “use this fallback, the coverage plugin isn’t installed” was ignored in three separate tasks, with the rule in context every time. The postmortem concluded that a rule which has failed three times as prose becomes a make target. The same thing happened with links left behind when a task file moves: the skill first got a paragraph with a workaround, and then the task tool learned to repoint the links itself. When an instruction keeps failing, I stopped writing a better paragraph and changed the mechanism.

The system also has to check itself, including its own checks. One postmortem wrote its lessons into the wrong checkout and then said they were in the commit. Nothing contradicted it, because the working tree looked clean. Now it has to confirm that each lesson’s file shows up in the right git status. Mutation testing reported kill counts that were fake, because tests that crashed were counted as kills. A green pytest line turned out not to be the gate’s verdict. And when a postmortem proposed two more rules for a single friction, it rejected them, with the reason written down: a skill that grows on every friction stops being read.

Then there are the checks that weren’t what they looked like. A shortcut that was safe when someone wrote it stopped being safe once things around it changed. A check ran on every change and still stopped nothing, because nothing was wired to listen to it. A guard added to a shared tool was bypassed by skills that called the tool directly. In each case the check existed and was documented, but it relied on an assumption that was no longer true.

Each time a failure moved from a paragraph into a mechanism, I could delegate a bit more.

From a repo for me to a repo others use

In April, other people made 1% of the commits. In May it was 18%, and in August 46%, with ten people besides me contributing that month. Thirteen people have committed so far. Use keeps spreading, slowly, to other teams and individuals, although most of the commits still come from a few of us.



What surprised me is that nobody came to “use Eduardo’s tools”. They came with their own problem: running our data pipelines, Snowflake operations, migrating services between platforms, alert noise per squad. The repo gave them context and a mechanism, and several of them then started improving the system: seven of the 45 skills were written by someone else, and one colleague launched an initiative to make the workspace’s context cheaper for every session.

None of them adopted the whole thing, and none of them had to. You don’t need to file tasks, record decisions or run the 14-phase flow to get value from the repo. The pieces are useful on their own and they compose: you can start by reading the knowledge base, pick up one skill weeks later, and register a task or a communication only when it helps. I suspect that’s a big part of why adoption happened without a mandate.

For people who are new to the repo, those open questions are usually the way in. With the context of the whole platform in one place, anyone can open a session and say “this is my situation, I want to do this, how is it done at Clarity?”, and get an answer grounded in our decisions, runbooks and code. A colleague who started using it recently told me it had given him more onboarding than any person had. That kind of use leaves almost no trace in git, so the charts undercount it.

The first time the tooling broke because I wasn’t its only user came in June, when two of us created different decision records with the same number, three times in a week. Sequential IDs assume a single author. Random suffixes on every ID fixed it: a small change, but one you only make when the tool has to work for more than one person.

Then I stepped away. Between 20 August and 1 September I made zero commits, and the repo got 191 commits from six other people.


On 6 September we recorded what was already true: the workspace is open to anyone at Clarity, and nobody has to go through me to use it or change it. I steward it: I maintain the tooling, review what lands on main and run the nightly loops. The deeper changes of direction still tend to come from me, mostly because that’s the easy path, not because anyone has to ask.

What I haven’t solved yet

Two problems grow at the same pace as adoption, and I don’t have good answers for either yet.

Integration with the company’s task system

The repo is the source of truth for our work, but the company runs on Jira, and keeping the two in sync is manual: a task here, its mirror ticket there, keys copied by hand. Many commits cite a Jira key in the subject line alone, and some exist only to say “mirror ticket created” or “comment posted”. One housekeeping skill exists only to stop GitLab from turning our DR-NNN and INC-NNN references into links to Jira tickets that don’t exist. I haven’t decided which direction the sync should go, or how to avoid double bookkeeping without breaking “everything is in the repo”. I’m running a few experiments on exactly that right now.

Pruning, cleaning and compacting the knowledge base

“Everything in the repo” also means everything accumulates. Since April, 602 knowledge documents have been added and 30 deleted, with a single explicit cleanup in July. The instruction file every agent session loads grew from about 430 words to about 4,600. Disk space is the least of it: every session spends part of its context on what nobody has pruned, and outdated knowledge is worse than missing knowledge, because an agent treats it as true. My idea is a weekly routine, like the health check, that detects duplicates, stale documents and contradictions with the code or with newer decisions, and proposes the compaction as a reviewable change. The agent proposes, a human decides. It’s not automated yet.

What I’m not claiming

Commits are activity, not value, and many are the workspace’s own bookkeeping. This is not a controlled experiment: one person driving it, better models arriving during the same months, people who were already hands-on. I haven’t compared the workflow against a small guide alone, so I can’t tell how much of the result is the system and how much is the model doing well by itself. The 191 commits from six people in the 13 days I made none tell me the repo works without me. They don’t tell me people would use it if I weren’t the one asking. Writing everything down has a real cost I feel but haven’t measured. And none of this is autonomous: a human approves every push and runs every destructive change, on purpose.

What I can say is how it feels from the inside. The feedback from the people using it has been very good, and I’ve never been this productive, above all on cross-cutting problems, the ones that touch many teams and repos at once and usually stall. That’s an impression, not a measurement, but it’s a strong one.

What comes next

In the next posts I’ll take apart some of the skill families and some of the subsystems behind them, like communications and task management. I’ll pick the order as I go.

And if you lead a platform or engineering team: which of these problems are you fighting right now?

  • Radical Detachment in the AI Era: Reinventing How We Build Software

item.title: [andros.dev] I built a forum with no interface, no passwords, made for the terminal
item.description:
I like forums. Debates, questions, answers, opinions, etc. That feeling of an asynchronous community, where answers are thought through and content lasts, is what makes the internet an interesting place. That is why I like reading them and taking part in them. But I had never designed or built one.

Maybe you have come across BBJ at some point, a bulletin board for the terminal built for small communities (tildes, pubnixes, club servers, etc.). I love its spirit. However, its foundations, architecture-wise, could be better. What would a modern bulletin board look like? In my spare time I started sketching one, and I ended up building my humble headless, federated forum, with simple, modern technologies and open standards.

As always, what matters is what you learn along the way. A forum looks simple, but it hides the classic problems of any server. Who can do what? How do you tell a moderator from a regular user? What happens when you have to ban someone? How do you stop someone from stealing an account? Roles, permissions, bans and security. I had to solve them one by one.

Let me tell you how I made Tyrtulia, but what I really want to explain are my decisions.

Why not use one that already exists?

Of course, before starting I looked at what was already out there. There are very complete free software forums:

  • Discourse: the most popular one today.
  • Flarum: PHP with MySQL.
  • NodeBB: Node.js, with MongoDB, Redis or PostgreSQL. It stands out for real time with WebSockets.

Or the good old classic: phpBB.

They are all fantastic, but they are designed to be used from a web browser. They also have an ambitious scope. That is ideal for large communities, but too much for a small, light forum.

A forum with no interface

The first decision was to build no interface. The server only offers a solid, documented API. It is REST with hypermedia: the client only knows one route, GET /, and discovers everything else by following links. And I banned myself from inventing my own formats. Underneath there are only some very boring standards:

  • RFC 9110: HTTP semantics, with ETag and If-Match so edits don't overwrite each other.
  • RFC 9457: errors.
  • RFC 7396: partial updates with PATCH.
  • RFC 6570: URL templates.
  • RFC 4287: Atom feeds.
  • RFC 9562: UUIDv7 identifiers.
  • JSON Schema: validation.
  • Server-Sent Events: real-time events.

There is no web interface, no forms, no advanced authentication systems, no file handling (images, attachments, etc.), and nothing that isn't strictly needed to read and write messages. Everything I left out was code I would never have to maintain.

That is why it is so light. It uses between 60 and 70 MB of RAM and about 50 MB of disk. It only needs Python and SQLite to run.

An API that discovers itself

How does a client know what it can do? The server tells it with links. Look at the same request, GET /, made by a guest (simplified):

{
    "name": "Forum of example.org",
    "_links": {
        "self": {"href": "/", "method": "GET"},
        "latest": {"href": "/threads", "method": "GET"},
        "search": {"href": "/search{?q,author,in}", "method": "GET", "templated": true},
        "login": {"href": "/sessions", "method": "POST", "schema": "/schemas/session"}
    }
}

And now by alice, logged in:

{
    "name": "Forum of example.org",
    "_links": {
        "self": {"href": "/", "method": "GET"},
        "latest": {"href": "/threads", "method": "GET"},
        "search": {"href": "/search{?q,author,in}", "method": "GET", "templated": true},
        "createThread": {"href": "/threads", "method": "POST", "schema": "/schemas/thread"},
        "notifications": {"href": "/notifications", "method": "GET"},
        "events": {"href": "/events", "method": "GET", "type": "text/event-stream"}
    }
}

If I change a route tomorrow, no client breaks, because none of them knew it in advance. They just follow the links the server gives them.

Along the way, this solved one of the problems I mentioned at the start: permissions. The client never asks whether you are a moderator. If you can edit, an edit link appears. If the thread is closed, reply disappears. And so I wouldn't cheat myself, Tyrtulia Web has a test that fails if I write an API route in the code.

No passwords

No OAuth, no OpenID, no sign-up forms. There are two ways to authenticate:

  • Your Unix user: the client talks to the forum through a Unix socket. The operating system tells the forum which user is on the other side. No sign-up, no login. Your user is your account.
  • SSH key: the client connects over HTTP and the forum sends it a challenge. The client signs it with your private SSH key and the forum verifies it with your public key.

There is no registration over HTTP. If you have a Unix user on the server, you already have an account: it is created the first time you connect through the socket. From there you can add your SSH keys to log in from outside. If you don't have a user on the machine, the administrator creates an account for you with your public key from the command line. On a tilde, having a Unix user is already the invitation.

A security detail you might find interesting: the challenge.

What would happen if the client signed the challenge and nothing else? Imagine you use the same SSH key on two forums, A and B, and A is malicious. A asks B for a challenge, pretending to be you, and sends it to you as if it were its own. You sign it without suspecting anything, and A uses your signature to log in to B with your account. It's a classic relay attack.

That is why the forum doesn't send the bare challenge, but a message that also carries its address and your username:

tyrtulia login
origin: https://forum.example.org
username: alice
challenge: 3q2-7wXbG0yTuFq8aN1sKkz9Jm5vQe4Lr6Hc2Pd0Tbw

Before signing, the client checks that origin is the forum it is talking to. If it doesn't match, it doesn't sign. That way a signature is only valid for one forum, one user and one challenge.

It's the same idea behind passkeys (WebAuthn): the signature is bound to the domain, so it's useless anywhere else.

And if someone has to be banned, their sessions are revoked and their keys are blocked.

Easy to use, secure, and no passwords to steal.

A modern BBJ

Before writing any code, I studied BBJ in depth. I wanted to know what to keep and what to change. Some things struck me. The password travels on every request as an unsalted SHA-256 hash, so in practice the hash is the password. And notifications have been pending since 2017.

First, the foundations.

BBJ Tyrtulia
API style RPC: everything is POST /api/<endpoint> REST with hypermedia (HAL): only GET / is known
Permissions The client asks (is_admin, edit_query) Links that appear or disappear
Authentication Unsalted SHA-256 hash of the password on every request No passwords: Unix socket or SSH-signed challenge
Errors 6 custom numeric codes RFC 9457 with a catalog of types
Pagination Everything at once Cursor based
Concurrency The last edit wins, silently ETag and If-Match
Text format Custom language ([bold: ...], [red: ...]) Standard Markdown
Validation A db_validate endpoint JSON Schema linked from each form
Configuration config.json TOML

Then, the features I missed.

BBJ Tyrtulia
Reply to a specific post >>N quotes in the text Linked replies, with a tree view
Mentions No Yes
Notifications No (pending since 2017) Inbox with replies, mentions and alerts
Real time No, you have to poll Server-Sent Events, with resume
Edit history No, editing overwrites Full, with diffs and revert
Deletion Deletes the row Tombstone: numbering is preserved
Search Each client searches what it has downloaded Server-side full text, accent and case insensitive
Feeds No Atom for the forum and each thread
Moderation Admin or not Roles, hidden posts, reports and a public log
Rate limiting No Per user and per IP

And what I left untouched, because it is what makes BBJ special:

  • A small server, easy to maintain, built on SQLite.
  • Several text clients against a documented API.
  • Reading without an account.
  • The tilde spirit: no images, no attachments and no categories.

Clients

A headless forum is useless without clients, so I had to write them.

Tyrtulia TUI

The first and most natural one was for the terminal.

Tyrtulia TUI is the terminal client, built with Textual.

tyrtulia.el

If you know me a little, you know this package was a must: tyrtulia.el.

Tyrtulia Web

Tyrtulia Web is more a mirror of the content than a client. Its goal is to let search engines index the forum and let anyone read it from a browser.

It has an unstyled theme and another one that mimics my website.

Federation

You can connect to one forum or set up several. Federation happens in the clients: servers don't talk to each other or copy messages between them. Each forum is independent, with its own users, rules and moderators.

Instead of splitting them into tabs or accounts, the clients mix the threads of all of them into a single list.

Of course, you can only write in the forums where you have an account. In the rest you can only read.

I think it's a pretty cool feature, because it keeps the API code much simpler and lets you explore other forums at zero cost.

What I take away

In short, it has been fun.

I also found out that it works for more than a forum. A thread can be a wiki page with its history, a pinned notice for every user on the server or an article in a group blog. And since a cron script can post through the socket with no credentials, you get a wall that doesn't get lost and can be searched.

Of course there are more complete forums, more powerful federation systems, and even decentralized systems that leave Tyrtulia in the dust (Aether, Nostr...). But its niche is very specific: a light, closed-access, federated, indexable, secure forum with text clients. For everything else, there are better things out there.

If you feel like trying it, the installation guide is in the Tyrtulia repository.

I look forward to your feedback.

item.title: [andros.dev] Where do I publish: HTTP, Gopher or Gemini?
item.description:
I agree with McLuhan: the medium, in this case the protocol, is part of the message. Switching protocols is not just a technical decision, it also changes the way people read. The audience is not the same. Neither is the time they spend reading you or exploring your site.

An HTML site carries a mental load: standards, a good DOM design, optimizations (like images), CSS styles, responsive design for different devices, etc. On Gemini or Gopher, on the other hand, you can afford to relax. You follow a syntax that is easy to remember or look up, and you focus on what you want to write. The reader relaxes too, because they know what they will find before they get there.

Answering the question is like choosing between a car and a bike. The bike is worse at almost everything: it is slower, carries less and you get wet. But the experience is personal: you maintain it yourself, you ride along small paths and you notice more of what is around you.

So, to answer the question:

  • HTTP: a large audience. Millions of sites, with very powerful browsers and lots of options.
  • Gemini: an indie audience, with friendly browsers like Lagrange.
  • Gopher: a technical audience, who almost always read from the terminal.

For me, the most amazing thing is the gift we receive from those who write in a Gemini capsule or a Gopher hole (gopherhole). They publish for a few dozen users in a niche. Their texts tend to have a very high quality or a freedom that is hard to find. They are not looking for visits, only to share, selflessly and with deep care for their work. They probably enjoy the journey more than their readers enjoy the result. It is so much like writing free software! You give without knowing who will receive it.

README.rst  generate_pigeon.py

To include them, add the (D) glob qualifier, which stands for “dot files”:

$ ls …

item.title: [hugovk.dev] Change macOS light and dark mode via command line
item.description:
I normally have my macOS set to dark mode because developer, but sometimes I need to take screenshots for talk slides. For readability and accessibility, it’s important to have enough contrast, and often dark text on a light background is best.

Aliases #

Rather than having to click 🍎 > System Settings… > Appearance > Light, here’s a couple of aliases to do it from the command line:

alias light-mode='osascript -e "tell app \"System Events\" to tell appearance preferences to set dark mode to false"'
alias dark-mode='osascript -e "tell app \"System Events\" to tell appearance preferences to set dark mode to true"'

Then I can type light-mode, take the screenshot, and then go back with dark-mode.

See also #

Some info on accessible presentations:

  • GOV.WALES: How to create accessible PowerPoint presentations

  • W3C Web Accessibility Initiative: Making Events Accessible
